analytic.title: RTISM: Real-Time Inter-VM Communication based on Shared Memory for Mixed-Criticality Flows

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Virtual machines (VMs) have been increasingly deployed in real-time systems to enhance heterogeneous resource sharing. Despite being isolated for security and prevention of failure propagation, VMs need to communicate with each other to complete certain tasks jointly. A real-time inter-VM communication framework has been proposed based on VirtIO, which is in essence a mechanism of message passing with high latency and low scalability on data amount. In contrary, IVSHMEM implements inter-VM communication with shared memory, which is generally fast and large in throughput. Unfortunately, IVSHMEM does not resolve resource contention between flows and hence cannot be applied in real-time scenarios. In this work, we propose a real-time inter-VM communication framework RTISM built upon shared memory and IVSHMEM. RTISM provides priority-based scheduling and supports mixedcriticality flows. Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT) analysis is reported to bound the end-to-end communication delay and a Limited Priority Assignment (LPA) algorithm is developed to enhance schedulability. Experimental evaluation shows that (i) RTISM has about 4 times higher throughput than the VirtIObased inter-VM communication framework; (ii) LPA improves schedulability by over 25% compared to the state-of-the-art; (iii) WCRT produces a tight bound.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: With the rapid development of semiconductor technology, the hardware of most embedded real-time systems has gradually changed from a microcontroller (MCU) to a Systemon-Chip (SoC) [1]. Based on the underlying support of SoC, the virtualization technology is widely used in 5G devices, automotive domain controllers, and medical instruments to enhance heterogeneous resource sharing. The virtualization technology allows one host computer to create and run multiple Virtual Machines (VMs) by virtually sharing the memory and CPU resources while ensuring security isolation between VMs [2]. For example, the cockpit domain controller in an intelligent automobile typically requires the deployment of two VMs: one VM is dedicated to the instrument system and another VM runs the infotainment system [3]. Although VMs are isolated for security and prevention of failure propagation, they still require necessary communication with each other (i.e., inter-VM communication) to complete some specific operations. For instance, in the cockpit domain controller, the instrument system (VM 1 ) displays the status information from the infotainment system (VM 2 ), while the infotainment system (VM 2 ) needs to obtain input signals from the instrument system (VM 1 ).

A simple way for inter-VM communication is using a network protocol, such as TCP/IP; however, TCP/IP needs to rely on the thick network protocol stack in the OS kernel. The VirtIO is a para-virtualization solution that can implement communication between the front-end VirtIO driver in the VM and the back-end VirtIO device in the host based on a ring buffer (i.e., VirtQueue) [4]. Based on the VirtIO, the latest realtime inter-VM communication framework was proposed by introducing the DMA (Direct Memory Access) transmission between back-end VirtIO devices. However, the VirtIO does not utilize the feature of sharing the same physical memory resource, leading to low communication performance [5].

IVSHMEM (Inter-VM Shared Memory) introduces a virtualized PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect) device for each VM [6]. Based on the IVSHMEM, the shared memorybased inter-VM communication is implemented because the PCI device of each VM can be mapped to the same memory address space of the host. Compared with the VirtIO, the IVSHMEM realizes a simple and fast inter-VM communication by shared memory [6]. However, IVSHMEM utilizes shared memory for communication without any scheduling mechanism or timing analysis. Hence, it cannot be deployed for real-time communication directly. Most real-time communication systems are mixed-criticality systems, where each flow has both priority and criticality, and all flows coexist in the same system [7]; considering the inter-VM communication in the cockpit domain controller, instrument-related flows are high-criticality flows and infotainment-related flows are lowcriticality flows. It is necessary to develop a real-time inter-VM communication framework for mixed-criticality flows to meet real-time information exchange in the embedded virtualized system.
This paper studies the real-time inter-VM communication based on shared memory provided by IVSHMEM. The contributions are below.

(1) We propose a real-time inter-VM communication framework RTISM built upon shared memory provided by IVSH-MEM in Linux KVM [8] (Kerneral-based Virtual Machine). Each VM contains a limited number of FIFO-based transmission queues (Tx-buffers) and receiving queues (Rx-buffer). Each transmission (or receiving) queue has a unique priority and the receiving queues are created in the shared memory. This design leads higher-priority flows to be sent and received first, resulting in low latency. It also enables RTISM to effectively handle mixed-criticality flows.

(2) Based on the RTISM framework, end-to-end Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT) analysis for inter-VM communication is conducted to bound the communication delay. We propose a Limited Priority Assignment (LPA) algorithm for enhancing the schedulability of mixed-criticality flows. "Limited" means that the system only has a limited number of priorities. LPA assigns mixed-criticality flows to this limited number priorities based on critical levels, deadlines, and periods to improve the schedulability of high-criticality flows and the service quality of low-criticality flows as much as possible.

(3) Experimental evaluation is carried out from three aspects: 1) the proposed RTISM framework has 4 times higher inter-VM communication bandwidth than the VirIO-based inter-VM communication framework; 2) the proposed LPA method has 25% higher schedulability than the latest TPA [9] (Targeted Priority Assignment); and 3) the comparison between theoretical analysis and practical measurement results shows the feasibility of the proposed RTISM and LPA.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work of inter-VM communication. Section III describes the system architecture and mixed-criticality flow model. Section IV presents the real-time inter-VM communication framework RTISM. Section V proposes the timing analysis and priority assignment for mixed-criticality flows in RTISM. Section VI conducts three experiments. Finally, we summarize this study in Section VII.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Ren et al. provided a comprehensive overview of the design choices and techniques for performance optimization of coresident (i.e., shared memory) inter-VM communication [10]. Gu et al. presented a comprehensive survey on real-time issues in virtualization for embedded systems [11]. In this section, we mainly review related works from two parts: 1) inter-VM communication; and 2) real-time inter-VM communication.

(1) Inter-VM communication. Huang et al. developed a shared memory communication library to implement the inter-VM communication based on the VMM (Virtual Machine Manager, i.e., hypervisor) bypass I/O model [12]. XenSocket [13] and XWAY [14] are two inter-VM communication schemes to realize shared memory-based inter-VM communication in the software stack from the socket and transport layers, respectively. MMNet [15] maps the kernel address space of a VM to the address space of its peer VM to achieve direct shared memory-based inter-VM communication. All the above works [12]- [15] are developed based on the Xen [16] hypervisor. On the KVM hypervisor, Wang et al. presented a zero-copy vhost design that modifies the extended page tables to achieve zero-copy data exchange [17]; however, this design only performs well when large packets are transmitted. VMPI [18] introduces a virtual device based on VirtIO to provide a simple message passing API, which can be used to implement a shared memory-based inter-VM communication on the KVM hypervisor. IVSHMEM [6] realizes shared memory-based communication by introducing a virtual PCI device in KVM hypervisor, and the experiments indicate that IVSHMEM outperforms VMPI [18] in terms of transmission performance. All the aforementioned works [6], [12]- [15], [17], [18] do not include the real-time communication into the inter-VM communication.

(2) Real-time inter-VM communication. [22]. Schwaricke et al. proposed a realtime VirtIO-based inter-VM communication framework on the jailhouse hypervisor; this framework introduces a broker at the hypervisor level to schedule communication flows and ensure real-time requirement [5]. As pointed out in Section I, VirtIO requires additional data migration technology (i.e., DMA) to achieve real-time inter-VM communication with an indirect manner, resulting in relatively low efficiency and high delay. In the following, we realize direct real-time inter-VM communication based on the IVSHMEM with a simple and fast transmission.

div.head: III. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND MIXED-CRITICALITY FLOW MODEL
div.p: In this section, we describe the architectures and model from the following parts: 1) the system architecture; 2) the IVSHMEM architecture; and 3) the mixed-criticality flow model.

div.head: A. System Architecture
div.p: Fig. 1 shows the system architecture of creating and running VMs on the x86-64 or ARM64 hardware platform by the QEMU/KVM virtualization framework. These VMs communicate with each other via shared memory provided by IVSHMEM. (1) The hardware used is based on a 64-bit CPU (Intel x86-64 or ARM64) with virtualization extension, and the host OS is the Linux operating system (Ubuntu 20.04).

(2) KVM (i.e., hypervisor) is a kernel module provided by the host Linux OS and is responsible for creating and managing VMs. /dev/kvm is a device that allows user-space programs such as QEMU to utilize the KVM kernel module through ioctl() system calls.

(3) QEMU (Quick Emulator) is a general-purpose opensource machine emulator [23]. QEMU can simulate hardware devices (e.g., Disk, NIC, USB, etc.) through software and run virtualization environments on different hardware and OSes. QEMU emulates hardware devices and invokes the KVM hypervisor to handle CPU and memory access, offering efficient virtualization technology support for VMs with nearnative performance.

(4) VM 1 and VM 2 communicate through shared memory provided by IVSHMEM. Although only two VMs are depicted in Fig. 1, multiple VMs are allowed to access the same shared memory. Since the communication is done through shared memory, sending flows means writing data to the shared memory and receiving flows means reading data from the shared memory.

div.head: B. IVSHMEM Architecture
div.p: IVSHMEM is a PCI device virtualized by QEMU. The IVSHMEM device memory on each VM is mapped to the same block of memory to provide a shared memory among the VMs. Simple and fast shared memory communication is achieved by reading and writing the shared memory. For the convenience of expression, the memory of the IVSHMEM device is regarded as IVSHMEM device. As shown in Fig. 2, IVSHMEM consists of four parts: 1) POSIX shared memory; 2) Virtual address space; 3) IVSHMEM PCI device; and 4) IVSHMEM device driver.

(1) POSIX shared memory. The POSIX shared memory on the host OS is the foundation of the entire shared memory system. It is created by the POSIX interface. The POSIX shared memory is mapped to the virtual address space of each VM through mmap().
(2) Virtual address space. The virtual address space is mapped from the POSIX shared memory and used to construct the ISVHMEM PCI device.

(3) IVSHMEM PCI device. The IVSHMEM PCI device is virtualized by QEMU and IVSHMEM device memory of each VM is mapped to its virtual address space through MMIO mechanism. By using MMIO, the process of accessing the IVSHMEM PCI device is the same as accessing memory.
(4) IVSHMEM device driver. The IVSHMEM device driver is a software interface that enables the kernel and applications to access the IVSHMEM PCI device.

div.head: IV. REAL-TIME INTER-VM COMMUNICATION FRAMEWORK
div.p: This section presents the RTISM framework, which is the real-time inter-VM communication framework based on the shared memory. The shared memory is provided by IVSH-MEM. We introduce the flow sending and receiving process as well as the implementation details of each component in the RTISM.

div.head: A. Overview of RTISM
div.p: A VM can act as both a sender and a receiver. To clearly explain the framework design, we take VM 1 as a sender and VM 2 as a receiver, as shown in Fig. 3.
(1) Sender (i.e., source-end VM). The sender includes three components: the dispatcher, the transmission queues, and the transmission engine, as shown in the left part of Fig. 3.

• Dispatcher. The dispatcher schedules the flow instances to be sent according to their priority and places them to the corresponding transmission queues to wait in line. • Transmission queues. The transmission queues are used to store the scheduled flow instances. The transmission queues are implemented with FIFO and priority. • Transmission engine. The transmission engine selects the appropriate flow instances from the transmission queues and sends them to the corresponding receiver. (2) Receiver (i.e., destination-end VM). The receiver includes two components of receiving shared memory and forwarder, as shown in the right part of Fig. 3.

• Receiving shared memory. The receiving shared memory serves as a buffer to store flow instances sent by other VMs to itself. The receiving shared memory is mapped from the shared memory (i.e., IVSHMEM) through mmap(). • Forwarder. The forwarder gets flow instances from the receiving shared memory according to priorities and passes them to the upper-layer application. The above five components work together to form a efficient real-time inter-VM communication framework. The details of transmission queues, transmission engine, and receiving shared memory are presented in the following subsections.

div.head: B. Transmission Queues (Tx-buffers)
div.p: The transmission queues are used to store the flow instances to be transmitted. As shown in Fig. 4, the transmission queues set up a total of 8 queues, which are Q tx 1 -Q tx 8 in turn. The transmission queues are implemented in the form of priority and FIFO.

(1) "Priority" means that each queue has a fixed priority, ranging from 1 to 8, where Q tx 1 has the highest priority of 1, representing the highest priority in the queue, and Q tx 2 has the priority of 2, representing the second highest priority, and so Fig. 4: Details of the transmission queues (Tx-buffers).

on. Priority ensures that flow instances with higher priority are sent first. For instance, as shown in Fig. 4, the f 2 has higher priority than f 3 and f 5 . f 2,1 and f 2,2 are sent before f 3,1 and f 5,1 (f 2,1 means the 1st instance of f 2 ).

(2) "FIFO" means that the flow instances in a queue are prioritized based on the time they are inserted. FIFO ensures that flow instances with the same priority that arrive first are sent first. For instance, as shown in Fig. 4, the f 3 and f 5 have the same priority of 4. Since
div.formula: f 3,1 joins Q tx 4 earlier than f 5,1 , it is sent before f 5,1 .
div.p: The advantage of using the combination of priority and FIFO scheduling mechanism in the transmission queues is as below: it provides not only a multi-priority representation of all flows but also an equal-priority representation of partial flows. We have chosen 8 queues in this implementation for future expansion and compatibility. For example, when extending to multiple devices, it can smoothly integrate with widely used technologies such as Time Sensitive Networking (TSN) [24] or Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) [25], both of which employ eight priorities (queues).

div.head: C. Transmission Engine
div.p: The transmission engine (middle in Fig. 3) selects flows from the transmission queues to transmit according to priorities. The specific process is as follows.

(1) The transmission engine always looks for the highestpriority queue with a ready flow. It selects the first flow instance in that queue to transmit. When the higher-priority transmission queue is empty, the transmission engine searches for the lower-priority queue.

(2) The process of transmitting a flow can be divided into the following steps (the relevant content of the receiving shared memory involved is presented in Section IV.D). 1) The transmission engine searches for the corresponding receiving shared memory according to the V M dest i of flow f i . 2) The transmission engine locates the receiving queue with the same priority as f i in the receiving shared memory. 3) The transmission engine obtains the write pointer from the control space corresponding to this receiving queue and determines whether the state of that data block pointed to by the current write pointer is 0. If the state byte is not 0, other VMs may be using this pointer currently. Therefore, the transmission engine adds 1 to the write pointer and determines whether the next state is 0. It should be noted that the value of the write pointer minus the read pointer cannot exceed the length of the receiving queue. 4) The transmission engine locates a data block that can be written to and sets its rw state to 1. It then increments the write pointer by 1 and updates the upper 6 bits of the status with its own VM ID. 5) The transmission engine writes f i into that data block. After completing writing, rw state is changed to 2, indicating that the writing is finished and the receiver can read it.

div.head: D. Receiving Shared Memory (Rx-buffers)
div.p: The receiving shared memory is used to store the flow instances sent to it by other VMs. Each receiver is allocated an exclusive memory area from the shared memory (a portion of the total shared memory), which is called the receiving shared memory. The size of the receiving shared memory can be adjusted freely (currently set to 16 KB). For example, VM 2 takes the part of the shared memory area whose offset address is 0x0000-0x3999 (the base address of the entire shared memory area has an offset address of 0) as its own receiving shared memory. (1) Receiving Queues. The receiving queues are similar to the transmission queues and are also implemented by using a combination of priority and FIFO. The receiving shared memory is divided into eight regions, each region is constructed as a FIFO ring queue. Each queue has a priority, Q rx 1 -Q rx 8 correspond to priorities 1 -8 respectively. Priority 1 is the highest, and priority 8 is the lowest. The first data block of each region is the control space. It stores the control information for maintaining the receiving queue. The control information mainly contains the write pointer and the read pointer. The write pointer indicates the next data block to be written, and the read pointer indicates the next data block to be read. The value of the write pointer is equal to or greater than the value of the read pointer and does not exceed the length of the receiving queue (the number of data blocks excluding the control space). By controlling the read and write pointers, the receiving queues become a ring queue logically.

(2) Data block. Each data block is 256 bytes in size, which is the minimum storage unit for a data packet (flow instance). As shown in Fig. 5, the first byte of a data block is the state byte, which is used to indicate the current state of the data block. The data segment is 255 bytes, which is used to store the flow instance content. If the size of a flow instance to be sent exceeds the limit of one data block, it will be split and stored in multiple data blocks with a method similar to IP fragmentation. The state byte consists of two parts: the high 6 bits are the ID of the source VM, and the low 2 bits are the rw state that represents the read-write status. The rw state has three possible values: 0, 1, or 2. Each value represents a different state: 1) 0 means that the data block is empty and can be written with a flow instance; 2) 1 means that the data block is being written with a flow instance to prevent duplicate or conflicting writes; and 3) 2 means that the corresponding data segment is valid and can be read.
(3) Read-write synchronization. For shared memory communication, read-write synchronization is a big challenge. We adopt two methods to achieve read-write synchronization:

• Setting the receiving shared memory of each VM as a separate area, such as VM 1 and VM 2 have independent shared memory as receiving shared memory. This ensures that only one VM reads the flow instance from the receiving shared memory, which is the owner of this receiving shared memory. • Using a state byte to indicate the state of each data unit, which determines who can access the data block. This ensures that only one VM can access a block unit at a time, either for reading or writing.

div.head: V. TIMING ANALYSIS AND PRIORITY ASSIGNMENT IN RTISM
div.p: In this section, we perform an end-to-end timing analysis of flows in the RTISM framework. Based on the timing analysis, we propose a new priority assignment algorithm LPA for mixed-criticality flows to enhance schedulability.

div.head: A. Worst-Case Response Time
div.p: Definition 1: Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT): The end-to-end worst-case response time R i is defined as the time elapsed flow f i from its triggering from V M source i to its reception by the forwarder module of V M dest i . The R i is calculated by
div.formula: R i = R source i + dest i . (3
R source i is the WCRT of f i its source-end VM (i.e., V M source i ), and R dest i is the WCRT of f i its destination-end VM (i.e., V M dest i ).
div.p: • R source i means the maximum time interval of the flow f i from the instant when f i is triggered in the V M source i to the instant when f i is sent to the receiving shared memory of V M dest i .

• R dest i means the maximum time interval of the flow f i from the instant when the flow is sent to the receiving shared memory of V M dest i to the instant when f i is received by the forwarder of V M dest i . R i less than D i indicates that flow f i is schedulable and meets the hard real-time requirement. For mixed-criticality flows in the system, if f i is a high-criticality flow, this means f i is real-time flow and need satisfy R i <D i ; if f i is a lowcriticality flow, we try to ensure R i <D i as much as possible to provide a better quality of service.

div.head: D. Priority Assignment Algorithm
div.p: The Optimal Priority Assignment (OPA) method proposed by Audsley [27] can address the problem of the priority assignments of flows. However, OPA has some defects and is not applicable to RT ISVHMEM: 1) The number of priority assignments in OPA is not limited, as each flow is assigned a unique priority; 2) OPA terminates when faced with unschedulability; and 3) OPA does not involve mixed-criticality flows.

In this study, we propose the two-stage LPA algorithm (Algorithm 1) to assign limited priorities for mixed-criticality flows in RTISM to improve the schedulability. In the first phase (lines 7-33), LPA performs an unlimited number of priority assignments and adopts the equal-priority placement strategy to enhance schedulability for mixed-criticality flow. In the second phase (Line 34), LPA invokes the limited priority reassignment (LPR, Algorithm 2) algorithm to evenly map the assigned unlimited priority to the limited priority. The proposed algorithm achieves: 1) Prioritize ensuring the schedulability of the high-criticality flows in the mixed-criticality flow; 2) Evenly assign priority for the mixed-criticality flow to prevent the unbalanced load of flows in different priority queues.

div.head: Algorithm 1 The LPA Algorithm

We create three sets to facilitate the LPA algorithm design:

• unassigned flow set is used to store the set of flows that are currently not assigned priorities, which means that the priorities of the flows in the set are higher than the current priority p. • assigned flow set is used to store the set of flows that are currently assigned priorities, which means that the priorities of the flows in the set are equal to or lower than the current priority p. • lep flow set is used to store the priorities of flows that are currently not assigned priorities, but it is assumed that the priorities of flows in the set are equal to or lower than the current priority p.
The details of LPA are below.

(1) Lines 1 -6. LPA first initializes these three sets and the currently assigned priority p. The initial value of p is the number of set F . Then LPA sorts flows in unassigned flow set according to their critical level (ascending), deadline (descending) and period (descending). This ensures that highcriticality flows are given higher priority and guaranteed schedulability in subsequent steps. For instance, the flows in

(2) Lines 7 -33. LPA loops assign appropriate priorities to flows in unassigned flow set by the equal-priority placement strategy. It assumes initially that there are no restrictions on the number of priorities.

Step 2.1: Lines 9 -15. LPA traverses sorted unassigned flow set in sequence to find a schedulable flow with the current priority. If there is a flow in unassigned flow set that is schedulable under p priority, update the flow and the corresponding set. For instance, as shown in Table II, the first polling finds that a flow can be scheduled is f 9 , assigning it the current priority of 10.

Step 2.2: Lines 18 -19. If there is no schedulable flow in unassigned flow set with priority p, the equal-priority placement strategy puts the first flow in unassigned flow set into lep flow set and updates the corresponding flow set. As shown in Table II, when priority 2 is assigned, and there are no schedulable flows available, the first flow f 8 in the unassigned flow set is moved to the elp flow set. At this point, f 8 is considered as an equal or lower priority flow than f 4 .

The equal-priority placement strategy assigns the current priority p to f j . If f j is schedulable, f j .schedulability is true, which means its priority must equal f i . div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we conduct the experimental evaluation from three aspects: 1) transmission performance comparison of different inter-VM communication schemes; 2) schedulability comparison between different priority assignment algorithms (i.e., TPA [9] and LPA); and 3) comparison of theoretical analysis and practical measurements.

div.head: A. Experimental Environment and Metrics
div.p: We conduct experiments in a real computer environment. The configuration of the computer is as follows: the CPU is an eight-core 2.40 GHz x86-64 Intel CPU with 2.40 GHz; the memory is RAM with a size of 16 GB; the virtualization framework is QEMU/KVM; the QEMU version is 6.2.0 and the Linux kernel version is 5.15; the Host OS is Ubuntu 20.04; the Guest OSes are Ubuntu 20.04. Each guest OS is allocated with 2 CPU cores and 2 GB RAM memory.
We conduct three experiments in this study, and each experiment uses an individual metric.
(1) The performance metric for Experiment 1 is communication throughput. The larger the throughput, the better the transmission performance.
(2) The performance metric for Experiment 2 is the acceptance ratio of flows, which is calculated by
div.formula: AR flow = NUM flow schedu NUM flow all . (13
div.p: NUM flow all is the number of all flows in the flow set, and NUM flow schedu is the number of schedulable flows. Once a flow instance times out, the corresponding flow is considered to be unschedulable. The higher acceptance ratio AR flow means that more flows is schedulable.
(3) The performance metric for Experiment 3 is the acceptance ratio of flow instances, which is calculated by
div.formula: AR instance = NUM instance schedu NUM instance all . (14
div.p: NUM instance all is the total number of flow instances in a given interval, and NUM instance schedu is the number of flow instances that satisfy the real-time constraints. Generally, the higher acceptance ratio AR instance means that more flow instances meet their individual deadlines. The purpose of using different acceptance ratios is to meet the needs of different computing scenarios.

div.head: B. Experiment 1: Communication Throughput Comparison of inter-VM Communication
div.p: The evaluation metric for this experiment is the communication throughput inter-VMs. Currently, the VirtIO [4] and Vhost-User with DPDK [28], [29] are two widely used inter-VM communication solutions, where the Vhost-User with DPDK is an acceleration technique based on the VirtIO. To compare the throughput, we conduct continuous data transmission tests between VMs using VirtIO, Vhost-User with DPDK, IVSHEMEM, and RTISM. The experimental results are obtained by averaging the communication throughput measurement values from 1,000 tests.

(1) As the Fig. 6 show, The throughput of the four schemes ranked from high to low is IVSHMEM (2154 MB/s), RTISM (1367 MB/s), Vhost-User with DPDK (368 MB/s), and VirtIO (75 MB/s). Communication through shared memory based on IVSHMEM is much more efficient than communication through the network interface provided by VirtIO. Because shared memory-based communication is simple and fast while VirtIO-based communication involves intermediate forwarding and a complex network protocol stack. The shared memory Fig. 6: Communication throughput comparison of inter-VM communication using four communication schemes. method bypassing the traditional TCP/IP protocol stack to realize inter-VM communication has three advantages: 1) reduce the number of data copies by shortening the data transmission path, 2) avoid unnecessary switches between VMs and hypervisor by reducing the dependency on the hypervisor, and 3) write data immediately by using shared memory.

(2) RTISM has excellent throughput exceeding 1 Gbps (1024 Mb/s), but it is slightly slower than IVSHMEM due to the addition of the real-time scheduling framework. In order to ensure real-time communication, we let the high-criticality flows guarantee the real-time constraints and increase the overall schedulability. The bandwidth loss in RTISM is acceptable because the final communication bandwidth can meet the practical application requirement.
This experiment confirms the excellent throughput of RTISM based on shared memory communication.

div.head: C. Experiment 2: Schedulabily Comparison between TPA and LPA
div.p: In this experiment, our flow set is extended from reallife data from General Motors [30], which contains multiple flows from applications such as active safety, engine control, and surround view. We set 32 flows with different attributes, including critical level, deadline, period, and size. The critical level is from 0 to 1; the deadline ranges from 2500 to 5000 μs; the period is from [1000, 2000, 5000, 10000] μs; and the size is 90 to 250 bytes. These flows are shown in Table III. All the flows are sent from VM 1 to VM 2 .

TPA [9] is the latest improved OPA algorithm for infinite priority assignment. We use LPA algorithm and TPA algorithm for priority assignment to compare the acceptance ratios of the flow instants. The results are presented in Tables IV, V, and VI.

(1) As can be calculated from Table V and VI, the acceptance ratio AR flow of the flow set LPA is 93.75%, while that of TPA is 68.75%. LPA has a 25.00% higher acceptance ratio than TPA. And the acceptance ratio of high-criticality and low-criticality flows of LPA is also better than TPA. When an unschedulable flow is encountered, TPA assigns it the current lowest priority. But LPA treats it as a potential schedulable flow with the same priority, this may reduce the number of higher-priority flows and make it schedulable.

(2) By comparing the acceptance ratio of high-criticality flows (100.00%) and low-criticality flows (87.50%) of LPA , it can be concluded that LPA firstly satisfies the schedulability of high-criticality flows, and the priority of high-criticality flows tends to be assigned a higher priority.

This experiment verifies that LPA can enhance the schedulability of flow aggregation and is friendly to mixed-criticality flows. LPA is an algorithm tailored for the RTISM and a suitable priority assignment algorithm for this system.

div.head: D. Experiment 3: Comparison of Theoretical Analysis and Practical Measurements
div.p: After assigning priorities of flows using LPA, we evaluate the acceptance ratio AR instance of the flow instances generated by the 32 flows shown in Table III. An important challenge for determining whether a flow instance has timed out is the clock synchronization problem between two VMs. The clock asynchrony between two VMs causes an error when testing whether the flow sent by VM 1 has timed out at VM 2 . This makes the final test result inaccurate. Even if time synchronization is performed by mechanisms like PTP (Precise Time Protocol) [31], there may still be a large difference between the TABLE III: Real-life extended flow set with 32 flows. (1) The results in Table VIII show that the acceptance ratio (100.00%) practically measured in VM 1 is closer to the theoretical value (92.36%) than the acceptance ratio (46.61%) practically measured in VM 2 . This difference could be attributed to clock asynchrony between the two VMs. The measurement method in VM 1 proposed introduces some time errors from receiving to acknowledging flow, but it can determine the timeout under the same system clock, and this error is smaller than directly assessing the timeout at the receiver. Therefore, we use the acceptance ratio practically measured in VM 1 as the result of the experiment.

div.p: (2) As shown in Table VII, for the acceptance rate of the high criticality flow, the actual measured value is 100% as the theoretical value; and for the low-criticality flow, the actual measured value (100.00%) is (15.28%) higher than the theoretical value (84.72%). This is because our response time analysis is based on worst-case scenarios, which rarely happens in practice.

From the above, it can be concluded that the actual experimental results are close to the theoretical results, which further verifies the correctness of the WCRT analysis. It also shows that the method proposed to measure response latency based on this framework is more accurate.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we develop a real-time inter-VM communication framework called RTISM on a KVM hypervisor, which realizes simple and fast inter-VM communication based on shared memory. The proposed RTISM resolves resource contention for mixed-criticality flows among VMs through priority-based scheduling, which achieves real-time transmission while still maintaining high communication throughput (over 1 Gbps). The proposed timing analysis method and priority assignment algorithm are effective in enhancing the schedulability of flows in the RTISM. Theoretical analysis and practical measurements confirm the feasibility of our method. RTISM provides a practical solution for real-time inter-VM communication in embedded virtualization systems, and it can be easily extended to other hypervisors. This shared memory-based scheduling framework and priority assignment algorithm also provide a reference for other scenarios that use shared memory for real-time communication, such as intercore communication on SoC or inter-chiplet communication.
